The talus acts as a load dampener between the rotational motion of the foot as it contacts the
ground and the linear advancement of the limb during the stance phase.
The combination of complex shape and articular coverage makes talar injuries uniquely
important.

Overview
The talus plays a key role in the mechanics of weight-bearing motion. Its position
between the foot and lower limb and the articulations it controls are vital for the normal
progression of gait and the adaptability of the foot to uneven surfaces. Loss of the
natural alignment of the talus may lead to considerable weight-bearing pain and gait
abnormalites1,2 (Resource 2).
Epidemiology
3% to 6% of lower-extremity bony injuries
Second most frequently injured tarsal bone

Epidemiology
Fractures of the talus are uncommon, representing less than 6% of all fractures
observed. Although rare, they may be devastating if missed or undermanaged. Many
injuries of the talus are the result of considerable trauma and can be easily missed in
evaluating a patient with multiple injuries. Among the tarsal bones of the foot, the talus
experiences more injuries, with the exception of the navicular.

The talus consists of a head, neck, and body; the body is divided for management purposes
into the main body, the lateral process, and the posterior process, which has a medial and
lateral tubercle.
The talus has five articulating surfaces, and 70% of its surface is covered by cartilage.
The talar body is trapezoidal in shape. The posterior end is narrower than the anterior end.
Provides bony stability in mortise with dorsiflexion
Has increased rotational motion in plantar flexion, requiring ligaments to control position
The lateral arc of the talar body in the tibiotalar joint is greater than the medial arc. The
tibiotalar articulating surface has a conical shape.

Because of its position between two major mobility joints—the ankle and the subtalar
complex—the talus has a unique shape, with cartilage covering almost 70% of its
surface. The talus has three main bony components: the talar body, talar neck, and talar
head. The body has two distinct processes known as the lateral process and the
posterior process. Both processes are areas of considerable ligament attachment. The
talar body articulates with the tibia, fibula, and calcaneus. The talar head articulates with
the navicular. The talar neck serves as the bridge between the talar body and the talar
head. The talar neck does not have an articular surface but serves as a major surface for
vascular access. It forms the tarsal canal between the middle and posterior facets of the
subtalar joint.
The talus has five distinct articulating surfaces. Two are located on the talar body and
three are with the head. The tibiotalar articulating surface is the largest and consists of
three articulating facets. The dome articulates with the tibial plafond. The medial and
lateral facets articulate with the tibial malleolus medially and with the fibula laterally.
The talar body is trapezoidal in shape, with the posterior or proximal end narrower than
the distal end. This allows for stable bony contact with the ankle in dorsiflexion and a
more flexible articulation in the ankle with the foot in plantar flexion. The major
tibiotalar articular surface has the shape of a cone, with its apex positioned medially. The
lateral radius of the talar body is larger than the medial radius. With plantar flexion and
dorsiflexion of the talus, the lateral side travels farther than the medial side, adding a
rotatory component to the up and down motion associated with the joint.
On the underside of the talar body is the posterior facet of the subtalar joint. The lateral
and posterior processes are found at this location. The posterior process may make up
as much as 25% of the posterior facet. The lateral process involves the articulations of
the anterior lateral corner of the posterior facet and the fibular facet of the ankle.
The talar head has three distinct articulations. The middle and anterior facets of the
talocalcaneal joint reside with the head. The major articular surface contacts the
navicular bone.

Vascular Anatomy3
The limited blood supply to the talus puts the talar body at risk for osteonecrosis after talar
neck fracture.
Blood supply enters the talus through capsular and ligamentous connections
Most of the blood supply to the body of the talus is from the artery of the tarsal canal, which
is located between the middle and posterior facets of the subtalar joint surfaces. It is fed by a
branch of the posterior tibial artery just proximal to the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
The deltoid artery in the deep portion of the deltoid ligament supplies blood to the medial
portion of the body of the talus. This is a branch of the tarsal canal artery and is fed by the
posterior tibial artery.
Most of the blood supply to the head and neck of the talus comes from the artery of the
tarsal sinus, a branch of the anterior tibial or dorsalis pedis artery and peroneal artery.

Vascular Anatomy
The vascular supply of the talus is important in that it is fed by all three major arteries to
the foot. However, because of limited access to the actual cancellous structure, it is
susceptible to vascular compromise if injured. Most of the vascular supply to the talar
body is from the posterior tibial artery, which feeds the artery of the tarsal canal. The
tarsal canal artery lies directly under the talar neck between the middle and posterior
facets. The artery also branches into the deep deltoid and serves as another access point
for vascular inflow to the talar body. The talar head and neck receive blood from the
dorsalis pedis and peroneal arteries. The perforating arteries are aligned in a radial
fashion in the capsular and ligamentous connections in the dorsal neck. The peroneal
and dorsalis pedis anastomosis in the sinus tarsi also supplies lateral flow to the head
and neck. Because of the unique vascular anatomy of the talus, avoiding detachment of
soft-tissue structures is important during surgical management of the talus.
Tendons
No tendons are attached to the talus.

tubercles of the posterior process.
The extensor digitorum brevis originates on the talus.

Tendons
The talus does not have any direct extrinsic motor connections. The flexor hallucis
longus tendon contacts the talus because it is supported by the medial and lateral
posterior processes of the talus as it changes direction to travel through the foot to its
insertion.
Joints and Ligaments
Anterior talofibular ligament: attaches along the lateral process
Talocalcaneal ligament: from the lateral process of the talus
Posterior talofibular ligament: attaches to the lateral tubercle of the posterior process of the
talus
Posterior talotibial or posterior deltoid ligament: attaches to the medial tubercle of the
posterior process
Deep deltoid ligament: attaches just under and anterior to the medial articular facet of the
talar body

Joints and Ligaments
The talus is rich with ligamentous attachments that stabilize or restrict talar motion
depending on the position of the talus. They also serve as potentially vital sources of
vascular inflow in patients with an injury; therefore, they should be identified and
protected during the management of these fractures.
Most of the major ligaments involved in talar motion attach to the talar body. Laterally,
the anterior talofibular ligament attaches along the lateral process surface and the
inferior anterior aspect of the fibula. The talocalcaneal ligament, which inhibits forward

posterior talofibular ligament attaches to the posterolateral process, and the posterior
talotibial ligament, which is described as a part of the deltoid ligament, attaches to the
posterior medial tubercle. The deep deltoid ligament is a major vascular supplier to the
talar body and runs from the deep tibial malleolus to just under the tibiotalar articular
cartilage of the talus.
Musculature
No major motor attachments to the talus exist.
Talar Neck Fractures
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Fractures of the talar neck occur with dorsiflexion of the talus against the tibia in combination
with an axial load, usually the result of a motor vehicle accident or a fall.2,4,5
Most often with medial comminution
Associated inversion with dorsiflexion may cause a fracture of the medial malleolus, whereas
eversion of the talus may be associated with fracture of the lateral malleolus.
Open injuries occur with considerable trauma to the soft tissues.
The talar body can be ejected from the wound. Preservation of the ejected part is important
for patient outcomes.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Talar neck fractures are the most common type of talar fracture and usually are the
result of considerable trauma. Often, they are found incidentally during a body survey in
a patient with multiple injuries. They also are observed with many recreational activities
and may be initially missed or managed as bad ankle sprains if the patient is not
carefully examined.

The neck fracture is associated with forced dorsiflexion of the foot at impact. The neck is
forced against the anterior tibia. Inversion or eversion forces during loading may lead to
malleolar fractures. Because of the unique configuration of the articular surfaces, any
displacement of the fracture may lead to subluxation or dislocation of one or more
joints.
After the stability of the bone is lost as a result of fracture, any additional deforming
forces on the foot may lead to considerable soft-tissue injury.
Expulsion of the talus can occur with severe trauma because no muscular layer aids in
prevention. Again, because of the unique function of the talus in weight-bearing gait,
location and preservation of any extruded part are important. Even in patients with an
open fracture-dislocation in which the talus is expelled from the body, recent literature
has shown satisfactory results if the extruded component is thoroughly washed and
securely replanted.6,7
Risk Factors
Because of the limited vascular anatomy and the proximity of the main vessels to the talar
body near the fracture, major disruption of the blood supply to the talar body may occur.
Injury Classification
Hawkins classification of talar neck fractures
Guides treatment decisions and helps predict the risk of osteonecrosis of the talus
Hawkins fracture types are based on displacement of the fracture and the articulations of the
talus.
Type I is a nondisplaced fracture of the talar neck.
Type II involves subluxation or dislocation of the posterior facet of the subtalar joint.
Type IIA: subluxation of the posterior facet
Type IIB: complete dislocation of the posterior facet
Type III involves subluxation/dislocation of the subtalar and tibiotalar joints.
Type IV is a type III fracture with talonavicular joint disruption.


Injury Classification
The Hawkins classification is the most recognized classification of talar neck fractures.
The classification is based on a particular joint surface being subluxated or dislocated.
Type I is a truly nondisplaced fracture of the neck, with no malalignment noted for any
joint surface. Passive full range of motion of the subtalar complex should be possible.
Type II involves displacement of the posterior facet of the subtalar joint. Type IIA denotes
less-than-complete dislocation, and type IIB denotes complete dislocation. This
subclassification was designed to indicate increased potential for vascular injury to the
bone. Type III fractures involve disruption of the subtalar and tibiotalar joints. Type IV is a
type III fracture with disruption of the talonavicular joint.
Although the Hawkins classification was initially developed to help classify the risk of
postinjury osteonecrosis, recent literature does not support the original hypothesis. The
risk of posttraumatic arthritis to the subtalar complex more closely follows the
classification of joint disruption.8-10
The OTA/AO classification of talar neck fractures essentially incorporated the Hawkins
classification into its numeric classification system. All fractures of the talus are
designated as 81. Talar neck fractures are designated as 81.2. The uppercase letter
corresponds with the Hawkins type and the lowercase letter denotes a simple versus
comminuted fracture.
Associated Injuries
May be part of high-energy trauma and easily missed if not actively investigated (Resource 3)
Peroneal tendon dislocation may occur.

Associated Injuries
Depending on the force applied to the limb, considerable injuries to the adjacent
structures and soft tissues may be present. Open injuries occur regularly if the talar

should carefully inspect the posterolateral malleolar area to ensure proper alignment of

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Should be suspected in any high-energy trauma involving an axial load to the lower extremity
Vehicular trauma from a head-on impact is to the result of the floorboard providing a
dorsiflexion-directed axial load.

Patient History
Any patient history that involves an axial load to the foot in a dorsiflexed position should
raise suspicion for a talar neck injury. Classically, talar neck fractures been described for
pilot injuries in a plane crash (aviator astragalus). Motor vehicle collisions in which a
head-on impact is involved is another frequent scenario. High-energy sports, such as
rock climbing, motocross racing, and mountain biking, also may result in talar neck
fractures.
Physical Examination
Any noted deformity of foot position or abnormal contour of soft tissue

that of the other foot. Any loss of symmetry in ankle or subtalar motion should raise
suspicion for a talar injury. Truly nondisplaced fractures may not be recognized until
weight bearing is attempted. Pain out of proportion to the initially suspected injury

Neurovascular Examination
Posterior tibial nerve and artery function should be evaluated if the talar body is displaced.

Radiography
Imaging studies in patients in whom talar neck fractures are suspected or possible should
include three radiographic views (AP, lateral, and oblique) of the foot. A mortise view of the
ankle also is advised to attain a complete view of the injury.

Radiography
Standard radiographs (AP, lateral, and medial oblique views) of the foot should be
routinely obtained if a talar injury is suspected. If possible, weight-bearing radiographs
should be obtained. For completeness, a mortise ankle should be obtained to evaluate
any extension into the talar body or potential ankle joint impingement.
A Canale view is obtained to more closely evaluate talar neck alignment. The view is
obtained by placing the foot flat on the collection plate. The x-ray beam should be 75°
higher than parallel to the collector or plate or, conversely, 15° perpendicular to the
collector and pointing toward the neck and body. The foot should be internally rotated

Computed Tomography
CT is routine in patients in whom a fracture is observed to clearly identify fragments and
displacement

Computed Tomography
In patients with a noted abnormality, CT is recommended to clearly identify the extent of
the injury to the neck and the surrounding structures. CT also is an important imaging
modality for planning the surgical approach and fixation.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be performed to evaluate the talar neck for subcortical fractures in patients with pain
but no detectable fracture line.
MRI can be used to detect osteonecrosis or osteocartilaginous fragments of the talus in later
stages of management.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The use of MRI acutely only has value if the clinician suspects a truly nondisplaced
fracture and must determine the source of pain to plan management. Edema in the neck
is the characteristic sign of a true type I talar neck injury. In the chronic setting, MRI may
illuminate the fracture line and any healing issues, such as osteonecrosis. Therefore,
many surgeons use titanium implants to minimize metal scatter in assessing for
osteonecrosis after management.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Closed reduction of a talar fracture can be attempted with the knee flexed by using plantar
flexion with varus or valgus angulation of the heel, depending on the direction of displacement
of the fracture fragments.2,4,5
This should be done only as a temporizing measure to reduce soft-tissue pressure.
Any displacement after closed reduction should be managed via open reduction.
Hawkins type I fractures are nondisplaced fractures of the talar neck and can be managed via
cast immobilization and non–weight bearing on the affected foot, with follow-up radiographs
obtained to confirm maintenance of reduction.

Nonsurgical Management
In the management of talar neck fractures, anatomic reduction of the fracture must be
attained and maintained to have the best likelihood of restoring normal ankle and
subtalar complex motion and alignment of the weight-bearing foot. Nonsurgical
management is reserved for type I fractures. Displacement in any vector may cause
considerable long-term dysfunction in weight-bearing activity.
This does not mean initial closed reduction does not have a role in the management of
talar neck fractures. In patients with tenting of the skin or malpositioning of the foot, an
initial attempt at a closed reduction may help reduce soft-tissue stress and allow for
adequate time for surgical planning. In the past, it was thought that urgent fixation was
necessary to achieve the best result and reduction of osteonecrosis; however, more
recent literature shows that osteonecrosis may not be related to timing of surgical
management. Urgent surgical management is not recommended in patients without
obvious soft-tissue compromise.
If a truly nondisplaced talar neck fracture is present, preservation of the position still is
important. The foot should be immobilized in a neutral position, and weight bearing
should be avoided for at least 6 weeks.

Surgical Management
Indications
Urgent surgical treatment is required in patients with an open talar fracture and in patients in
whom subluxation or dislocation may result in soft-tissue compromise (Resource 4; Videos1, 2
and 3).
Closed reduction is recommended to take pressure off skin if deformity is present.
Talar body extrusion also is considered urgent.
If present, the body should be cleaned and replanted with internal fixation.
Hawkins type I fractures may be managed with the use of screws inserted percutaneously in
a posterior-to-anterior or anterior-to-posterior direction if early motion is desired.
Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) should be performed for all displaced fractures
(Hawkins type II, type III, and type IV).
Surgical management is not urgent for closed fractures without soft-tissue compromise.
Allow time to perform adequate imaging studies.
Allow the soft tissue to settle from the initial trauma.
Recent literature suggests waiting until the soft tissue is stable and imaging studies are
complete; does not increase the rate of talar osteonecrosis.


Surgical Management
Early literature categorized talar neck fracture surgical management as urgent/emergent
because of the perceived risk of substantial osteonecrosis if surgical management was
delayed. More recent literature has not shown this to be true; however, urgent surgical
intervention may be necessary in certain situations. By definition, open fractures are
urgent and should be washed and fixed as expeditiously as possible. In most centers,
adequate time exists to obtain a CT scan before surgical management to fully
understand the fracture pattern and the position of joint disruption. In patients with
talar body extrusion, the extruded component should be thoroughly washed in a series
of sterile water baths to remove all contaminants and then replaced and stabilized to the
neck, followed by appropriate wound closure and management.
For closed fractures in which the talar body is dislocated, tenting of the soft tissues
usually is present, which may lead to local tissue hypoperfusion and considerable
compromise. If simple, closed reduction does not reduce pressure on the soft tissue,
then urgent surgical management should be performed after obtaining a CT scan to fully
understand the injury. Waiting a few days to allow the patient’s condition to stabilize and
to ensure no threat to the soft tissue exists does not increase the risk of osteonecrosis
and tends to decrease complications from repeated injury to the soft tissue, such as
wound healing and infection. In every patient, rigid internal fixation is recommended to
maintain anatomic reduction. Bone graft may be necessary to fill any void in the bony
structure caused by comminution.4,6,7
Preoperative Planning
CT is preferred to ensure no associated fractures or intra-articular comminution is present.

Preoperative Planning
A preoperative CT scan is highly recommended to ensure no intra-articular fragments or
associated fractures exist that were not observed on plain films because of bony

Patient Positioning
ORIF of talar neck fractures is best performed with the patient in the supine position.
Place a bolster under surgical leg to facilitate positioning
Fluoroscopy arm from the opposite side of the table

Patient Positioning
Typically, the patient is placed in the supine position for visualization, reduction, and
fixation. The surgical leg is elevated on a bolster so the contralateral leg will not interfere
with lateral fluoroscopic views. The knee should be bent to remove the tensile force of
the triceps surae. This will improve the surgeon’s ability to manipulate and gain visual
access to the subtalar and ankle joints. A tourniquet may be used at the calf or thigh.
Surgical Approaches
A two-incision approach usually is used to achieve accurate reduction of the fracture (Figure
4).
The anteromedial approach is between the posterior and anterior tibial tendons.
The anterolateral approach usually parallels the extensor longus tendons and permits direct
visualization of the dorsal and lateral walls of the talar neck to assess rotation. It also allows
for direct access to the lateral talar body.
In patients with a fixed dislocation of the subtalar joint, a third posterolateral incision may be
necessary to gain access to the lateral subtalar joint and manually release the subtalar
impaction to enable the body to reduce.
A threaded Steinman pin also may be used as a joystick in the talar body to disimpact the
subtalar facet.

A two-incision surgical approach is recommended in reducing talar neck fractures. The

with the fourth metatarsal bone. Superficial peroneal nerve branches may traverse the
incision and should be protected. From this position, the lateral side and dorsal side of
the neck and the lateral non-articular portion of the talar body are observed. The
anterior subtalar joint also can be observed and débrided if necessary. With both
incisions, accurate rotational alignment and axial alignment are possible.

After talar neck fractures were initially described and a classification system was

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Talar head injuries are the least common talar fracture. Talar head injuries result from
an axial load transmitted through the foot rather than the lower leg (as described for
other talar injuries). The position of the fracture lines in the talar head depend on the
position of the navicular at the time of loading. A centrally positioned navicular will result
in a comminuted burst-type fracture of the talar head. A medially positioned navicular or
an inverted foot will result in a shear fracture of the medial aspect of the talar head and
an impaction injury to the lateral, uncovered portion of the foot. A laterally positioned
navicular or an everted foot result in create a shear fracture of the lateral portion of the
talar head. This portion of the talonavicular joint remains congruous and impacts against
the uncovered portion of the joint. All three of these scenarios may result in a locked
subtalar joint complex. In addition, substantial potential exist for collateral injuries to the
calcaneus, cuboid, and navicular itself.

The patient is best treated in the supine position for a talar head fracture. Elevation of

The vascular supply to the talar head is mainly through the capsular attachment around

dissection of the capsule is important to preserve supply. Visualization of the fracture
site is important for reduction. The talar head is a somewhat spherical surface, and
accurate reduction via indirect means, such as a C-arm, is difficult. A longitudinal incision
should be made over the fracture site to facilitate direct visualization for disimpaction

head, the use of a small external fixator between the navicular or cuneiform bones and
the calcaneal tuberosity should be considered to distract the joint.
Fixation of the reduced fragments is accomplished with mini-fragment screws, which are
used to fix the loose fragment to the stable part of the talar head to which the neck is
still intact. Most of these screws are placed percutaneously to minimize soft-tissue
stripping and achieve good fracture compression. In patients with complete articular
dissociation of the talar head with the neck dorsal, mini-fragment plating may be
necessary to stabilize the reduction. Based on the integrity of fixation, placement or
retention of the external fixator may be beneficial to resist the normal compressive
forces at this joint and prevent late collapse or shortening. Accurate reduction and
fixation is confirmed after satisfactory full range of subtalar complex motion is restored.
